questions.stem: A 75-year-old man presented with fever, sepsis, and a painful left cheek. He had a history of diabetes treated with metformin. He had an ultrasound that revealed no abscess in the parotid. He was started on broad treatment with vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam along with volume resuscitation and was admitted to the ICU.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is the most common cause of suppurative parotitis. Diabetic and elderly patients are at higher risk for developing parotitis. An antistaphylococcal agent would be indicated as empiric coverage.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q10

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis underwent bilateral lung transplant under alemtuzumab induction. The patient was known to be colonized with Aspergillus fumigatus preoperatively and received posttransplant antifungal prophylaxis with voriconazole. Her immediate postoperative course was complicated by acute kidney injury requiring hemodialysis. On postoperative day 18, the nurse noted a 4×6 cm left buttock decubitus wound with a black eschar. There was no surrounding erythema. Excisional debridement was performed. The underlying gluteus muscle was necrotic and liquefied. An organism grew on Sabouraud agar after 4 days of incubation. Microscopy demonstrated broad hyphae without septa. Rootlike hyphae were also noted.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Decrease immunosuppression and perform serial wound debridements
Measure serum voriconazole concentration and adjust the antifungal dose accordingly

questions.explanation: Switch to liposomal amphotericin B The microscopic finding of nonseptate hyphae is consistent with an agent of mucormycosis. Rhizoids (rootlike hyphae) are typically produced by Rhizopus spp. Voriconazole has no activity against Rhizopus. Breakthrough infections while on voriconazole prophylaxis have been reported. Renal failure requiring hemodialysis is a risk factor for the disease. Hospital outbreaks have been associated with the use of contaminated linen which may have been the source in this case. Amphotericin B in combination with adequate surgical debridement is the treatment of choice. Treatment can be stepped down to posaconazole or isavuconazole after clinical improvement. However, initial therapy with an azole as a single agent is not recommended. Lomentospora prolificans (formerly Scedosporium prolificans ) is inherently resistant to all antifungals. Lomentospora forms septate hyphae with branching similar to Aspergillus spp.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q29

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman was reviewed with a 3-week history of fevers and a 1-week history of painful skin nodules. She was known to have a persistent neutropenia following an allogeneic stem cell transplant 4 weeks earlier for relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She had been taking levofloxacin, voriconazole, valaciclovir, and trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis; the levofloxacin had been switched to intravenous cefepime 3 weeks earlier, but her symptoms had progressed. On examination, her temperature was 103°F (39.4°C), her blood pressure was 110/68 mmHg, her heart rate was 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturations 98% on room air. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. There were multiple subcutaneous purplish popular and nodular lesions of various sizes scattered throughout her extremities, her neck, and her chest. Some of the lesions had central necrosis. She had pedal onychomycosis. Investigations: Total white cell count 0.2 ×109 /L (4–10) Absolute neutrophil count 0.0 ×109 /L (2–8) Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL (13–17) Platelets 43 ×109 /L (150–400) eGFR>60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Blood cultures at admission were negative, but repeat blood cultures at the point of review 3 weeks later were positive for a mold.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fusarium solani Fusarium are species of mold that may cause disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients. It tends to be more resistant to the azole antifungals than Aspergillus species but sensitive to amphotericin. Disseminated fusariosis may be identified through positive blood cultures. The typical clinical picture is as described in a patient with prolonged (>10 days) neutropenia, persistent fevers, widespread skin lesions that evolve rapidly, and blood cultures growing a mold. Unlike aspergillosis, blood cultures are commonly positive. Mortality rates are high even with appropriate antifungals and immunotherapy such as G-CSF . Because the pathogen identified is a mold, Candida tropicalis, Histoplasma capsulatum, and Cryptococcus neoformans would not be the answer, as they appear as yeast forms in the human body. However, these pathogens can cause disseminated nodular skin lesions in immunocompromised patients. Aspergillus fumigatus is not the correct answer, as voriconazole is usually effective prophylaxis against invasive aspergillus infections, and aspergillus rarely is identified in blood cultures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q39

questions.question: Pulmonary mucormycosis: outline the treatment, risk factors, and microbiology features.

parts.text: Pulmonary mucormycosis - treatment, risk factors, and microbiology features.

parts_raw.text: Pulmonary mucormycosis - tx, risk factors, microbiology features

questions.model_answer: a) Risk factors: pulmonary mucormycosis is most common in (1) prolonged neutropenia; (2) hematologic malignancy; (3) allogeneic HSCT and, less often, solid-organ transplant recipients; (4) deferoxamine therapy for iron overload; contributing factors include high-dose glucocorticoids, hyperglycemia/diabetic ketoacidosis, and acidosis. Microbiology features: Mucorales are thermally monomorphic molds that grow rapidly on fungal media; in tissue they show broad (uneven diameter, 3-25 um), thin-walled, empty, mostly aseptate (pauciseptate) hyphae with focal bulbous dilation and nondichotomous, irregular branching at occasional right angles; culture recovery from tissue is poor owing to hyphal friability, and identification to genus rests on rhizoid development, sporangium shape, and sporangiospore location (MALDI-TOF/PCR increasingly used). They are inherently resistant to voriconazole and fluconazole, to the echinocandins, and to flucytosine. Treatment: (1) reverse predisposing factors (control hyperglycemia, reverse ketoacidosis, taper glucocorticoids); (2) urgent surgical debridement/resection, which improves survival over antifungals alone; (3) first-line high-dose lipid amphotericin B (L-AMB, commonly 5 mg/kg/day, up to 10 mg/kg/day) started without delay; (4) step-down/salvage with posaconazole (extended-release tablet or IV, 300 mg) or isavuconazole once responding.

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: Malnutrition, patients receiving deferoxamine for iron overload, haemodialysis. Microbiology: broad ribbon like hyphae, non septate, rapid growth, thermally monomorphic, produces spores in round sporangium. Treatment: AmphoB deoxycholate, isovuconazole, posaconazole, debridement (if possible). Inherently resistant to several azoles (ketoconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole), flucytosine (5-FC) and echinocandins

questions.question: Your patient has recently undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplant and presents with a lung nodule. Lung biopsy shows a Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain. [image-based question: GMS stain of lung biopsy] Contrast Zygomycetes (Mucorales) and Aspergillus species by completing the table.
questions.question_raw: Your patient has recently undergone HSCT and presents with a lung nodule. Lung biopsy is undertaken showing the following (a Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain). [image-based question: GMS stain of lung biopsy] Please contrast Zygomycetes and Aspergillus species and complete this table (note: the table content had no relation to the photo or clinical vignette above).

parts.text: Complete the table (Organism: Zygomycetes / Aspergillus) for hyphae thickness, angle of branching, and septate or aseptate.

parts_raw.text: Complete the table (Organism: Zygomycetes / Aspergillus) for: Hyphae thickness; Angle of branching; Septate or aseptate

questions.model_answer: a) Hyphae thickness: Zygomycetes (Mucorales) - broad, wide, uneven diameter (3-25 um), ribbon-like; Aspergillus - narrow, uniform width (approx 3-5 um). Angle of branching: Zygomycetes - wide, nondichotomous, irregular branching at occasional right angles (approx 90 degrees); Aspergillus - regular dichotomous branching at acute angles (approx 45 degrees). Septate or aseptate: Zygomycetes - mostly aseptate (pauciseptate); Aspergillus - septate.
questions.beyond_mandell: Aspergillus values (narrow ~3-5 um, acute ~45 degree dichotomous branching, septate) are the standard histopathology contrast; Mandell text describes the Mucorales side directly.

questions.question: Antifungal question.

parts.text: What component of the cell membrane do azoles inhibit synthesis of?
Which antifungal agent is Pichia kudriavzevii (formerly Candida krusei) intrinsically resistant to?
A patient is infected with Candida auris and has had no prior exposure to antifungal agents. What class of antifungals would you use empirically?
Name THREE antifungals active in the treatment of mucormycosis.

parts_raw.text: What component of the cell-wall do azoles inhibit synthesis of?
Which antifungal agent is Pichia kudriavzevii (formerly Candida krusei) intrinsically resistant to?
A patient is infected with Candida auris. They have had no prior exposure to antifungal agents. What class of antifungals would you use empirically?
Name THREE antifungals active in the treatment of mucormycosis.

questions.model_answer: a) Ergosterol (azoles inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis; the question states "cell wall" but ergosterol is a cell-membrane sterol). b) Fluconazole (intrinsic azole/fluconazole resistance). c) Echinocandins (e.g., caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) - first-line empiric therapy for C. auris given frequent azole resistance. d) Any three of: (1) liposomal amphotericin B, (2) isavuconazole, (3) posaconazole.
questions.beyond_mandell: C. auris empiric echinocandin therapy reflects CDC guidance.

questions.question: A man with acute myeloid leukemia receiving chemotherapy has two large cavitary lung lesions with associated brain lesions.
questions.question_raw:
Q19 (2007) Brain + Lung lesions
Man with AML getting chemo with 2 large cavitary lung lesions

parts.text: Voriconazole is started and he develops sinus necrosis. What is the organism?

parts_raw.text: B) Voriconazole started, develops sinus necrosis. Organism?

questions.model_answer: a) Three possible causes of cavitary lung lesions in a neutropenic AML patient: (1) Aspergillus species (invasive pulmonary aspergillosis); (2) agents of mucormycosis (Mucorales); (3) Nocardia species (other reasonable answers: bacterial - Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, anaerobes/Streptococcus anginosus; or Mycobacterium tuberculosis). b) Agents of mucormycosis (most commonly Rhizopus) - breakthrough infection is characteristic when fungal sinusitis with necrosis develops on voriconazole, which lacks activity against Mucorales. c) (1) Rapid reversal of predisposing factors and, in neutropenia, consider granulocyte transfusion/G-CSF; (2) urgent surgical debridement; (3) high-dose lipid amphotericin B first-line, with step-down to posaconazole or isavuconazole once improving.
questions.beyond_mandell: The bacterial/TB/Nocardia items in the cavitary-lesion differential are established knowledge; Mandell grounds the Aspergillus and Mucorales entries and the voriconazole-breakthrough point.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Bacterial: S. anginosus, Anaerobic (oral flora), TB, Nocardia, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae. Fungal: Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Mucormycosis.

B) Agents of mucormycosis: Rhizopus species (47%), Mucor species (18%), Cunninghamella bertholletiae (7%), Apophysomyces elegans (5%), Lichtheimia (Absidia) species (5%), Saksenaea species (5%), Rhizomucor pusillus (4%).

C) Surgery; Ampho B; Posaconazole when improving/oral stepdown.

questions.question: A neutropenic patient with acute myeloid leukemia presents with sinusitis and a necrotic palate.
questions.question_raw: AML neutropenic patient with sinusitis and necrotic palate

parts.text: What are 4 (of 10) risk factors, other than neutropenia?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 (of 10) risk factors, other than neutropenia?

questions.model_answer: a) An agent of mucormycosis (Mucorales) - most commonly Rhizopus species; the necrotic palate eschar extending from the maxillary sinus is classic for rhinocerebral mucormycosis. b) Four risk factors (of many): (1) diabetes mellitus, particularly with diabetic ketoacidosis; (2) hematologic malignancy; (3) hematopoietic stem cell or solid-organ transplantation; (4) high-dose glucocorticoid therapy (others: deferoxamine/iron overload, hyperglycemia, acidosis, trauma/burns, IV drug use, malnutrition). c) (1) Rapid correction of predisposing factors (control hyperglycemia, reverse ketoacidosis, taper glucocorticoids); (2) urgent surgical debridement of infected sinus/palate tissue; (3) first-line high-dose lipid amphotericin B, stepping down to posaconazole or isavuconazole once responding.

cohort_answer.text: Mucormycosis - Rhizopus oryzae, Rhizomucor, Mucor, Cunninghamella (agents of mucormycosis: Rhizopus most common 47%, Mucor 18%, Cunninghamella bertholletiae 7%, Apophysomyces elegans 5%, Lichtheimia 5%, Saksenaea 5%, Rhizomucor pusillus 4%). Risk factors: Diabetes (poorly controlled, especially with DKA); Transplant (HSCT, SOT); Steroids (high dose corticosteroids); IVDU; metabolic acidosis; heme malignancy; penetrating trauma/burns; iron overload/chelation therapy with deferoxamine (no longer used). Treatment: Urgent surgical debridement; Liposomal AmB first line (5mg/kg daily) for several weeks; then step down to posaconazole or isavuconazole when improvement seen.

questions.question: Agents of mucormycosis (Zygomycetes): list several and give the treatment.

parts.text: What is the treatment for each?

questions.model_answer: a) Five agents of mucormycosis (Mucorales): (1) Rhizopus (e.g., R. arrhizus/oryzae); (2) Mucor (e.g., M. circinelloides); (3) Rhizomucor; (4) Lichtheimia (formerly Absidia); (5) Cunninghamella (others: Apophysomyces, Saksenaea). b) Treatment is essentially the same for all: urgent surgical debridement plus reversal of predisposing factors, with high-dose lipid amphotericin B (L-AMB) as first-line therapy for every species, since amphotericin B is the most active agent against Mucorales. Step-down/salvage is with posaconazole or isavuconazole, but azole activity is species-dependent: Cunninghamella shows higher amphotericin B MICs, and M. circinelloides has high isavuconazole MICs (often above achievable serum levels), so azole reliability is lowest for these. Echinocandins and flucytosine are inactive; a lipid amphotericin B plus echinocandin combination improved survival in R. arrhizus animal models but combination therapy has shown no survival benefit over timely L-AMB monotherapy in clinical series.

cohort_answer.text: Zygomycetes: Rhizopus, Rhizomucor, Cunninghamella, Mucor, Lichtheimia. Treatment: L-AmB for all, +/- echinocandin for rhizopus oryzae (evidence retrospective, no evidence of superiority over amphoB monotherapy, all patients were debrided). Urgent surgical debridement; Liposomal AmB first line (5mg/kg daily) for several weeks; then step down to posaconazole or itraconazole once improvement seen.

questions.question: A man has a skin infection; staining shows broad aseptate hyphae.
questions.question_raw: A guy with a skin infection that is stained and shows broad aseptate hyphae.
questions.model_answer: a) Cutaneous mucormycosis (broad, thin-walled, mostly aseptate hyphae are characteristic of Mucorales). b) First-line antifungal therapy is high-dose lipid amphotericin B (L-AMB, 5-10 mg/kg/day), with step-down to posaconazole or isavuconazole once the infection is responding. c) Additional/adjunctive management: (1) excision and wide surgical debridement of the cutaneous/soft-tissue lesion; (2) correction of underlying predisposing factors (control hyperglycemia, reverse ketoacidosis, taper glucocorticoids, discontinue deferoxamine); (3) adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen has been reported by some, though clinical evidence is not convincing, and granulocyte transfusion/G-CSF in neutropenia.

cohort_answer.text: Cutaneous mucormycosis. Treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B 5-10mg/kg IV q24h initially; step down to posaconazole (300mg PO BID x2 doses, then 300mg PO daily) once responding, or isavuconazole for oral step-down; duration not clearly outlined, treat until better (often prolonged). Other treatment: Surgical debridement; correction of underlying risk factors; control of hyperglycemia; reversal of ketoacidosis; rapid tapering of glucocorticoid therapy; discontinue deferoxamine if on it (not clearly shown to benefit); G-CSF if neutropenia.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man with SLE on prednisone and cyclophosphamide presents with multiple cavitary lung nodules and CNS nodules.
questions.question_raw: 32M with SLE on Pred + Cyclophosphamide who presents with multiple cavitary lung nodules and CNS nodules.

parts.text: List three pathogens that can cause this picture and the treatment for each.

parts_raw.text: List 3 pathogens that can cause this picture and treatments for each

questions.model_answer: (1) Nocardia (e.g. N. asteroides/N. farcinica) - high-dose TMP-SMX, adding imipenem +/- amikacin for severe/disseminated CNS disease. (2) Aspergillus / invasive mould - voriconazole (liposomal amphotericin B or isavuconazole as alternatives). (3) Cryptococcus neoformans - liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction, then fluconazole consolidation/maintenance. (Other reasonable answers: disseminated M. tuberculosis; Mucorales - liposomal amphotericin B plus surgical debridement.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Organism-specific therapy from Mandell chapters on Nocardia, Aspergillus and Cryptococcus / IDSA guidelines; this general chapter names these opportunists but not their treatment.
